/uk-news/2026/nov/18/doctor-whose-eviden.headline: New evidence feeds growing expert challenge to Lucy Letby convictions
/uk-news/2026/nov/18/doctor-whose-eviden.bodyHtml:
A senior doctor whose evidence helped to convict Lucy Letby and who was held up by prosecutors as a pre-eminent expert was barred from treating patients during the trial because of concerns that he posed a risk to their safety.

Prof Peter Hindmarsh, a specialist in hormones in children, was crucial to the crown’s argument that the British nurse had poisoned children by injecting insulin into fluid bags. But a Guardian investigation can reveal he was excluded from clinical practice in March 2023, five months before the end of the trial, by his employer, University College London hospitals trust (UCLH). Jurors were never told.

Letby, who was a neonatal nurse at the Countess of Chester hospital, was convicted of murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven others, and sentenced to 15 whole-life terms in prison. Court of appeal judges turned down her applications to appeal.

She has always maintained she is innocent, and her lawyer Mark McDonald has applied to the CCRC to send her case back to the court of appeal.

Since the convictions, dozens of leading UK and international medical experts have argued that the prosecution’s case, including Hindmarsh’s evidence, was wrong, and produced reports submitted in support of her CCRC application.

Dr Shoo Lee, a renowned Canadian neonatologist who argues that the prosecution misrepresented his research, last year made public the summary findings of a 14-member expert panel he had convened. They found unanimously that the babies died or collapsed due to natural causes and poor medical care on the unit, and that there was no evidence of murders, insulin poisoning or any other deliberate harm.

Seven experts have contributed to reports submitted by McDonald to the CCRC, contesting Hindmarsh’s opinions. They argue that Hindmarsh’s calculations and diagnoses of the babies’ medical conditions were factually inaccurate in many respects, and his opinion that insulin was infused via the fluid bags is not supported by the evidence. The experts also argue that blood tests known as immunoassays, relied on by the prosecution as definitive evidence of poisoning, are known to be fallible.

Lady Justice Thirlwall, who chaired a two-year public inquiry after the convictions, refused to consider the experts’ arguments that Letby may have suffered a miscarriage of justice, or to wait for the CCRC decision. She produced a report in September making a series of recommendations for the NHS, on the basis that Letby was guilty.

Among the reasons for UCLH’s decision was that his advice to child patients relating to insulin was not considered safe. A UCLH medical director told the General Medical Council (GMC), the doctors’ regulator, that the hospital could not “accept the level of risk Professor Hindmarsh appears to pose to children and young people”.

The GMC, which was already investigating Hindmarsh’s fitness to practise, subsequently applied for his registration as a doctor to be suspended. That could have resulted in his evidence in the trial of Letby – which was still in progress – being dismissed.

However, in April 2023 a medical practitioners tribunal – an independent panel that decides GMC proceedings against doctors – opted not to suspend his registration. Instead, it ordered that Hindmarsh be directly supervised in his work, to protect patient safety. That decision had no practical effect because UCLH had already barred him from practising at all.

While Hindmarsh’s ability to practise was being restricted, the trial of Letby continued at Manchester crown court. Her defence team was never informed that Hindmarsh’s hospital considered his professional judgment and practice so deficient as to be unsafe to child patients, or of the April 2023 tribunal ruling.

While Hindmarsh did inform the local police force, Cheshire constabulary, in December 2022 that he was subject to a GMC investigation, and in February 2023 the Crown Prosecution Service told Letby’s defence, her legal team was not made aware that he was later barred from practising on safety grounds.

Had they known, Letby’s defence team might have challenged his credibility as an expert witness and applied for the jury to be told or for his evidence to be dismissed.

Failures of disclosure are recognised as potential grounds for a referral to the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC), the miscarriages of justice watchdog, and for convictions to be overturned.

The apparent lack of transparency could mean Hindmarsh breached legal rules requiring expert witnesses to disclose to the party instructing them any disciplinary proceedings against them and anything that may be considered to undermine their credibility. Hindmarsh declined to answer any of the Guardian’s questions about this, the hospitals’ concerns about him, or the GMC investigation.

The insulin expert

Hindmarsh was presented to the Letby jury throughout as a distinguished authority. The lead barrister for the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), Nick Johnson KC, described him to jurors as “the pre-eminent expert” on insulin.

Hindmarsh was a consultant paediatric endocrinologist – a specialist in hormones, including insulin, in children – at UCLH from 1991, and a professor at UCL, with an eminent reputation.

When Johnson introduced Hindmarsh at the trial, he asked if he was also an honorary consultant at Great Ormond Street. The jury was not told that four months earlier, in July 2022, Hindmarsh’s contract in that role at the children’s hospital had been terminated.

Hindmarsh asserted in his trial evidence that blood tests and the medical records of two babies being cared for at the Countess of Chester hospital showed they had been poisoned with insulin, most likely inserted into intravenous fluid bags. The prosecution alleged that Letby injected insulin into the bags, although there was no direct or forensic evidence that she or anybody else had done so.

Hindmarsh’s evidence alleging insulin poisoning was considered pivotal to the convictions. In summing up, the judge, James Goss, told the jury that if they were sure babies were being deliberately harmed, they could decide other babies were also being harmed, even if they were not sure about the precise cause.

Johnson presented the two cases of alleged insulin poisoning as incontrovertible evidence. The charges of attempted murder of those two babies were the first on which the jury reached guilty verdicts, and two of only three unanimous guilty verdicts.

‘Multiple and wide-ranging concerns’

The Guardian first revealed in March that the GMC launched an investigation into Hindmarsh on 25 November 2022, the same day he first gave evidence as an expert for the prosecution of Letby.

Great Ormond Street hospital had reported “multiple and wide-ranging concerns” to the GMC, including Hindmarsh’s “diagnosis and treatment of patients” and “cases where harm to patients has been alleged”. UCLH had been leading a formal investigation of its own into Hindmarsh, and in December 2022 it reported its similar concerns to the GMC.

Then in January 2023, while the Letby trial was still ongoing, a medical tribunal imposed orders that while the GMC investigation continued, Hindmarsh could only work at UCLH, and his clinical work had to be supervised, because otherwise he “may pose a real risk to members of the public”.

Until now, it has not been publicly known that UCLH reported further serious concerns on 15 March 2023, and informed the GMC it had excluded Hindmarsh from treating patients at all. This was less than three weeks after Hindmarsh had given his second and final day of evidence at Letby’s trial, on 24 February.

Documents seen by the Guardian show that a UCLH medical director, Dr Tim Hodgson, informed the GMC of the hospital’s decision. Hodgson wrote that Hindmarsh had breached the supervision order and given independent medical advice relating to three child patients, two involving insulin and diabetes. Hindmarsh’s medical colleagues had submitted “written concerns” about him, Hodgson said.

“On the grounds of safety UCLH are not presently in a position to allow Professor [Hindmarsh] to practice clinically even under supervision,” he wrote. “… I do not believe UCLH can accept the level of risk Professor Hindmarsh appears to pose to children and young people even with close clinical supervision.”

In two of the cases, Hodgson said Hindmarsh had independently advised the families that the children stop being given insulin at home. One of the children had an episode of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), a critical, life-threatening complication caused by a severe lack of insulin.

“The patient had an episode of DKA and it’s not clear whether this coincided with the alleged advice from Professor Hindmarsh,” Hodgson wrote.

In the two insulin cases, Hodgson highlighted concerns that Hindmarsh was over-focusing on rare causes of hypoglycaemia (low blood sugar) and diabetes (a cause of high blood sugar). In the first case, his colleagues believed Hindmarsh was not addressing more common causes of diabetes, and in the second, that he was “not treating high glucose levels appropriately”.

Had Letby’s defence team been informed of this, it could have strengthened the case for an application to inform the jury or exclude Hindmarsh’s evidence.

Experts who have provided reports for Letby’s CCRC application have argued that Hindmarsh’s opinion that the babies were poisoned via their fluid bags was an extremely unlikely explanation for their condition. They argue that Hindmarsh failed to recognise more common, identifiable medical causes.

Hodgson also said Hindmarsh had questioned the reliability of an insulin antibodies blood test result, sharing “his concern with the family that this was an erroneous, fallible test”.

This too could have been significant to Letby’s defence. At the trial, Johnson presented results from the immunoassay blood tests as definitive and said there was “no doubt” the two babies were poisoned.

Experts supporting Letby’s CCRC application say immunoassays are known to be fallible because they can react to antibodies in blood to give a falsely high insulin result. Hodgson’s report suggests Hindmarsh recognised that some blood tests were fallible, but he never made this clear at Letby’s trial.

The duty to disclose

The GMC responded to these new concerns by applying to the tribunal for Hindmarsh’s registration as a doctor to be suspended. Hindmarsh’s barrister argued strongly that although he would not be treating patients because UCLH had excluded him, he should be allowed to continue working as an expert witness. Suspension, she said, would impede his ability to do so.

The barrister argued to the tribunal that Hindmarsh had not breached the supervision order and “no harm has been caused to patients”.

The three-person tribunal said it could not determine whether the previous supervision order had “technically” been breached. “However, the tribunal felt that the three cases identified by UCLH did raise concerns about patient safety,” it said.

The tribunal decided that to suspend Hindmarsh would be disproportionate and explicitly allowed him to continue working as an expert witness, saying its order should not “restrict his non-clinical work”.

Instead, it imposed a tightening of the supervision requirement so that Hindmarsh from then had to be directly supervised when treating patients. This appears to have been a theoretical measure, however, because Hindmarsh was already restricted to only working for UCLH, and the hospital had barred him from treating patients at all.

Expert witnesses have a legal duty under the criminal procedure rules to tell the party instructing them – in Hindmarsh’s case, Cheshire constabulary – anything “that might reasonably be thought capable of undermining the expert’s opinion or detract from the credibility or impartiality of the expert”. This includes any disciplinary proceedings by a regulatory body.

The rules were introduced in 2014 to improve the reliability of expert evidence and guard against miscarriages of justice, after a series of wrongful convictions in the late 1990s and 2000s.

Lawyers have told the Guardian that under the rules, Hindmarsh should have told the police of the April 2023 tribunal ruling and that his hospital had barred him from clinical practice.

Tim Green KC, a specialist in disclosure, told the Guardian: “Whilst I cannot comment on the facts behind this complex and sensitive case, it is clear that the duty of an expert witness to make disclosure in a criminal or civil case of all material capable of undermining his opinion or detracting from his credibility is a continuous one.

“This duty extends after he has given evidence and through to the end of the proceedings. The duty continues through to any appeals, and arguably remains extant now, during the current considerations of the CCRC.

“Further restrictions imposed by a professional disciplinary tribunal on an expert’s right to practise, like those which can be imposed by the medical practitioners tribunal, are also disclosable in my view. Such restrictions are likely to be relevant to an assessment made by a jury or judge of an expert’s opinion evidence, competence and skill. For the same reasons, it also arguable that the information which led the tribunal to impose those restrictions in the first place is also disclosable.”

Lawyers have said Hindmarsh may have had a duty to tell the police and CPS initially, earlier in 2022, of the investigation into his practice led by UCLH, and that Great Ormond Street had terminated his contract. He does not appear to have done so.

When Johnson, the lead prosecutor, first introduced Hindmarsh in court on 25 November 2022, he sought to clarify that the professor had an eminent position at Great Ormond Street as well as UCLH. After two questions not answered clearly, Johnson asked Hindmarsh: “Are you an honorary consultant at Great Ormond Street hospital though?” Hindmarsh replied: “Yes. At that stage, yes.”

Hindmarsh did not say his contract at Great Ormond Street had been terminated four months earlier. That point was never clarified to the jury.

Hindmarsh was first informed of the GMC investigation into him on 30 November 2022. By this point, he had already made his first appearance in the Letby trial.

He told Cheshire constabulary two weeks later, on 14 December 2022. The CPS was informed two months later and told Letby’s then barrister, Ben Myers KC, on 20 February 2023, just four days before Hindmarsh was due to give his second day of evidence.

The CPS told Myers it would oppose the jury being told, because the GMC investigation into Hindmarsh had not reached a final adjudication. Myers did not then make an application to the judge for the jury to be informed.

On 23 February 2023, the day before Hindmarsh was due to return and give evidence, Johnson reminded the jury about him. “Professor Peter Hindmarsh will be here tomorrow to deal with the issue of insulin,” Johnson said. “And because he’s the pre-eminent expert in that narrow field, we will call him first.”

In July 2023, the judge referred to Hindmarsh’s evidence in his summing up. He did not mention Great Ormond Street at all, describing Hindmarsh as “emeritus professor of endocrinology at University College London and also a consultant paediatric endocrinologist at University College London hospitals”. Apparently unknown to the judge, UCLH had excluded Hindmarsh from practising as a consultant four months earlier.

Letby was convicted in August 2023. The GMC investigation into Hindmarsh never reached a final determination. In November 2024 Hindmarsh applied to remove himself from registration as a doctor. The GMC allowed this, a process known as “voluntary erasure”, which meant the investigation was stopped with no final adjudication.

The CPS has confirmed to the Guardian that it did not disclose to the defence anything relating to Hindmarsh being barred from clinical practice or the April 2023 tribunal ruling, because it had not been made aware of it.

Cheshire constabulary declined to provide information to the Guardian, so it is not clear whether Hindmarsh did or did not tell the police. Either way, it was not passed to the CPS, which would have disclosed it to Letby’s defence.

“Cheshire constabulary will not be commenting further in relation to this case,” a spokesperson said.

A CPS spokesperson said: “The CPS met all its disclosure obligations and no objections were raised by the defence at any stage in relation to expert evidence relied on by the prosecution.”

The CPS’ statement is made on the basis that it disclosed what it knew to the defence, and it had not been told about the tribunal ruling or that Hindmarsh was barred from treating patients. Johnson’s representatives did not reply to questions from the Guardian.

McDonald, Letby’s lawyer, said: “Peter Hindmarsh’s evidence was pivotal to the prosecution’s case against Lucy Letby. The insulin allegations were not simply another part of the prosecution’s case; they were its cornerstone, presented as scientific proof that she had deliberately poisoned babies and was capable of murder.

“It shaped the jury’s perception of Lucy and provided the lens through which they were invited to view every other allegation. This was not evidence that could be neatly confined to two convictions. Its influence permeated the entire trial. If the foundations of the insulin cases are unsafe, the consequences for the safety of the wider convictions cannot be overstated.”

The Guardian asked Hindmarsh detailed questions about the hospitals’ concerns, UCLH excluding him from clinical practice, and the GMC investigation, and put to him that he appeared not to have made adequate disclosure under the criminal procedure rules.

A representative for Hindmarsh replied: “He has no comment in relation to these questions and points.”

/politics/2026/nov/18/eu-uk-reset-summit.headline: UK and EU near reset deal on food, emissions trading and youth mobility
/politics/2026/nov/18/eu-uk-reset-summit.bodyHtml:
The UK and EU are closing in on a reset deal due to be signed off at a summit on Friday, covering food and agriculture, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme. But diplomats have said the EU will shut the door to discussions with Andy Burnham about the UK's longer-term relationship with the bloc until the government has decided whether it wants to proceed with reversing Brexit.

European capitals are also warning they have reached the end of the line for piecemeal 'reset' summits with the UK and want the prime minister to focus on his next steps domestically before they proceed.

But they suggested a joint statement after the summit would signal that further discussions would follow on the UK's entry to the EU's energy single markets, irregular migration and a closer defence and security relationship.

'Clarity is what we need more than anything from the UK. Don't come back until you know what you want. Work out what your options really are and then come to negotiate,' one EU diplomat said.

'The prime minister needs to bring the public with him. We can't have another negotiation based on just half the country. We'll only put the effort in if we know it's not going to change down the line.'

Burnham is expected to set out his own next steps after the summit on Monday, including his hopes for a 'national conversation' on what a closer relationship might look like.

With less than 48 hours before the Brussels summit, negotiators were still racing to finalise Friday's agreement. A leaked draft seen by the Guardian shows continued disagreement over demands by the EU that the UK commit to aligning with the bloc's trade defence measures, such as tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, in exchange for inclusion in Made in Europe legislation.

The text shows the UK is pushing for a weaker commitment, only promising an 'aim to protect supply chains consistently across our markets and guard against potential risks of circumvention'.

A Cabinet Office source said Made in Europe language was 'the highest jeopardy' in the negotiations, while an EU official suggested it was the part of the discussions most likely to go 'down to the wire' on Friday.

Though there is a formal commitment to annual reset summits, senior EU diplomats say the current approach, designed by Keir Starmer, will quickly 'reach its limits' and more 'mini deals' do not make sense.

One said the 'piecemeal approach is coming to an end' and that Burnham's intentions for the UK's long-term relationship created a natural juncture for the EU too.

Another said: 'It is like a buffet: you can choose to nibble on one or two dishes to start, but at a certain point you have to go for the whole of the buffet.'

One EU diplomat said there would be a 'pause for reflection' after the Friday summit.

Burnham has said there is no rush to decide on the longer-term relationship, as he comes under pressure from within his own party to slow the pace of pursuing closer ties.

He is not now expected to set out the full range of options for the future relationship – the status quo, customs union, single market or full rejoin – until he announces his 10-year plan in December.

Sources said the government was considering holding a year-long 'national conversation' in 2027, including town halls and citizens assemblies, before deciding which route to pursue in advance of the next election.

However, the potential length of that debate has alarmed Brussels officials, who were caught off-guard by the launch of the new pro-Brexit campaign group Stay Out, set up by architects of the Vote Leave campaign.

One EU diplomat said: 'The government would spend the year making evidence-based arguments about each of the four options, while Boris Johnson and Michael Gove and Nigel Farage will spend it shouting about traitors.'

After the reset deal is agreed on Friday, it will be enacted by the European partnership bill, covering the deals on food and agriculture, emissions trading and youth mobility. It is expected to be introduced before Christmas, with legislation laid possibly as soon as next week.

EU diplomats said the two sides were expected to settle on a quota of about 100,000 people a year being allowed to work, travel or study in each other's territories. Originally, the UK had pitched for 50,000 and then 80,000, while Brussels has consistently sought a higher number.

Both sides have agreed that tuition fees for European students coming to the UK should be discussed at a later date, although there have been attempts by some member states to link the debate to the ratification of the whole reset deal.

Senior Labour figures are already beginning their push to have a full rejoining on the table. The former business secretary Peter Kyle said Burnham should fight the next election on a promise to rejoin the EU, with voters given a referendum on the outcome of any deal.

Kyle, who was a key member of Starmer's cabinet, said the 'only way through' the challenges of the domestic political debate was for the government to offer voters the choice to accept or reject any agreement.

He is the latest senior Labour MP to publicly wade into the Brexit debate, after the former foreign secretary David Lammy said the party should go into the next election clear that its intention was to rejoin.

Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, has also said Britain's future should be back in the bloc, arguing that leaving had made the UK 'poorer, weaker and less secure'.

/world/2026/nov/19/kerch-bridge-crimea-r.headline: Ukraine strikes symbolic Kerch bridge for third time in a week
/world/2026/nov/19/kerch-bridge-crimea-r.bodyHtml:
Ukraine's military has struck the Kerch bridge linking annexed Crimea to Russia for a third time this week, in what a source in its armed forces called a campaign designed to embarrass Vladimir Putin on the world stage, hours before he is due to meet Xi Jinping and Donald Trump in China. A Russian-appointed regional governor said traffic had been halted again on Wednesday while the new damage was assessed.

'Following a new attack on the Crimean Bridge, traffic has been temporarily halted. All relevant services are on site and at work. An assessment of the damage is under way,' Sergei Aksyonov, the Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, wrote on Telegram.

The bridge, which links Russia with Crimea, seized from Ukraine in 2014, is highly symbolic. A 227-metre section of the road spanning the Kerch strait was destroyed this week, but the rail corridor appears to be operable despite sustaining some damage.

'The bridge is a symbol of Putin's rule. Destroying it sends a message to the other two great leaders that Putin is not as strong as he pretends,' the source in Ukraine's armed forces said, of this week's attacks.

For Ukraine, the bridge is a hated symbol of Russian arrogance and colonial thinking. Ukraine has previously declared that the bridge across the Kerch strait, built eight years ago, is illegal. Kyiv had tried twice to blow it up – with a truck bomb in 2022, and a sea drone the following year.

Earlier, Ukraine critically damaged the road section of the bridge in what President Volodymyr Zelenskyy hailed as an 'unprecedented' military operation. A span of the bridge's road section collapsed, but the railway line was still standing.

Zelenskyy described the earlier attack as the culmination of a long and complex campaign to demolish the bridge, involving domestically produced drones and ballistic missiles. Palianytsia drones hit the road section of the bridge, while Neptune and other missiles targeted the adjacent rail section, he added.

/news/2026/nov/18/uk-government-russell-.headline: Ministers and tech firms move to shut down Russell Brand's social media
/news/2026/nov/18/uk-government-russell-.bodyHtml:
The British government, Meta and Google have all acted to limit Russell Brand's ability to broadcast from prison. Meta has disabled his Instagram and Facebook profiles, and a justice minister has reportedly asked Google to deactivate his YouTube account, according to Sky News, after he published a message claiming his innocence following his conviction for rape and sexual assault.

Earlier this week, the Ministry of Justice launched an investigation into whether Brand, 51, broke prison rules after he shared a message claiming he was not guilty days after his conviction at Southwark crown court.

He was sentenced to 10-and-a-half-years in prison for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

His wife, Laura Brand, read a message from her husband on Sunday in a video uploaded to their YouTube channel.

Prisoners are allowed to protest their innocence, meaning that no criminal offence was committed in the release of the video. However, convicts are not permitted to make statements from jail that cause distress to victims, and heavy restrictions apply to speaking to the media.

If he is found to have broken the rules, Brand could face sanctions ranging from an extension of his sentence to loss of privileges such as access to a phone for a limited period.

It is understood a prisoner will be deemed to have broken the rules if they provide comments to a family member that they know will be published.

Responding to the video, the prime minister's spokesperson called the comments 'clearly appalling'.

The education secretary, Lucy Powell, also criticised broadcasters on Wednesday for 'amplifying' Brand's words by airing a clip of Laura Brand reading the message.

She told LBC radio: 'I was appalled at that, and actually I think mainstream media shouldn't have transmitted that either.'

Asked why she wanted to censor the message, Powell said: 'It's a platform I don't think … should have been amplified, to be honest.'

The Ministry of Justice and Google were contacted for comment.

Google stopped Brand from profiting from YouTube content in 2023 after a media investigation revealed allegations of rape and sexual assault. At the time, the video platform said the decision was made 'to protect' its users.

/technology/2026/nov/18/anthropic-share-.headline: Anthropic prices shares above range, in position to surpass SpaceX's record IPO
/technology/2026/nov/18/anthropic-share-.bodyHtml:
Anthropic set the share price for its debut on the US stock market at $83 on Wednesday, positioning the artificial intelligence company for one of the biggest initial public offerings in history. The firm is slated to begin trading on Thursday under the ticker symbol ANT, with CEO Dario Amodei and other co-founders ringing the bell to open the Nasdaq exchange.

The pricing is above Anthropic’s earlier estimates. Last week, the San Francisco-based company, founded in 2021, set its preliminary share price at $70 to $78. With all shares counted, those prices put Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO) from $1.26tn to $1.41tn. Elon Musk’s SpaceX debuted on Wall Street in June with the biggest market offering ever at $1.77tn. With Anthropic setting its share price at $83, it could now surpass SpaceX.

Amodei is planning to sell about $260m worth of shares with the IPO, as are his six fellow co-founders. At the top of the price range, the co-founders’ stakes will be worth more than $18bn each.

When Anthropic filed for its IPO last month, the company detailed rapidly rising revenue in its prospectus: $41m in 2023, $386m in 2024, $4.585bn in 2025 (an increase of more than 1,000%), then $16.286bn in the first six months of 2026 alone. The company disclosed that, as of the end of June, it had raised $141.1bn.

Despite the increasing revenue, Anthropic disclosed a net loss of $80bn for the first half of 2026.

Anthropic’s main expenditure listed in its investor prospectus is computing power from datacenters. The company has compute purchase commitments and lease agreements of more than $70bn over the next 12 months and more than $450bn by 2030, with a further $450bn due by 2045.

Anthropic is the first company at the forefront of the generative AI boom to go public, and its performance is likely to affect investors’ enthusiasm. Its competitor OpenAI was slated to hit Wall Street later this year, but CEO Sam Altman has said that the company opted to delay its IPO until it can overcome safety concerns.

Anthropic’s IPO comes during a volatile time for AI and the stock market. Last month, the industry saw a broader slowdown, with share prices dropping at several companies amid growing concern about the technology. Then, last week, Nvidia, which designs the chips AI companies use to power their chatbots, was racked with a scandal that led to CEO Jensen Huang resigning after reports of multiple extramarital affairs.

/culture/2026/nov/19/florence-pugh-respo.headline: Florence Pugh calls for kindness after suing over fake surgery images
/culture/2026/nov/19/florence-pugh-respo.bodyHtml:
Florence Pugh has said she is 'disturbed' by a flurry of 'stressful' online speculation about her appearance after images of her at the Governors awards this week went viral.

The 30-year-old actor wrote a lengthy statement to her 11 million Instagram followers on Wednesday in which she denied speculation that she had undergone cosmetic surgery or used weight-loss injections.

'I find it so stressful waking up and have thousands of people talking about you and your body in ways that you can't even comprehend,' she wrote.

'I woke up the other morning and quite a lot of you were discussing my face and body in such a disturbing way. I learnt online that I had been on Ozempic? I learnt that I'd had upper bleph[aroplasty]? Lower bleph? Filler? Face lipo[suction]? Buccal fat remover? Chin surgery? Nose surgery?!'

The Dune, Thunderbolts and Oppenheimer actor continued: 'Yes, I'm disturbed. For women who now think that I'm someone I'm not. For having my body dissected and pointed at again.

'I have spent my whole career defending and protecting bodies that just grow the way they grow. I was subjected to fat shaming in the business from the moment I started and I have loved every time I get to tell someone they are being inappropriate about my weight, and I'm not changing that now just because you've all said so.'

Pugh, who is known for speaking out about beauty standards and scrutiny of women's bodies in Hollywood, insisted she had not undergone cosmetic procedures.

'I have never been on Ozempic, I have NEVER done any face surgery. And don't EVER say that I didn't make my own nose,' she wrote. 'I've always had that beautiful ski slope. Even as a baby!'

Pugh said she had made a series of lifestyle changes since turning 30, including 'chang[ing] my relationship with alcohol and to be able to do at least one pull-up in the gym.'

'It's funny to see you all use reference images from times where I was really mentally unhappy and abusing my body, and put it next to the image from the Governors awards the other night where I am happy and truly respecting my body,' she wrote.

'For the first time in my ENTIRE career, I have had the opportunity to be rested, to sleep, to wake up and work out and to eat regularly and healthily.'

Pugh said she had worked hard to improve her physical and mental wellbeing, adding: 'I'm looking after myself, and that's literally it.'

Reflecting on the criticism she has faced throughout her career, she said: 'I've always been aware that seeing a confident woman be happy in her skin is triggering to a lot of people and for a long time just accepted that I will receive commentary like that.

'But now this…? I'm asking us all to just be mindful. We are real people, living real lives.'

Pugh also claimed she had sued several publications earlier this year, claiming they published AI-generated images appearing to show her receiving cosmetic injections that were presented as real photographs.

'I was fucking horrified,' she wrote, claiming the articles had damaged her reputation.

Pugh concluded by urging followers to reflect on their attitudes towards physical appearance and the pressures of changing beauty standards.

'But please be gentle to yourselves and others when you go in on people's physical appearance,' she wrote. 'I'm not angry at you, I'm angry at the situation that's being projected onto us.

'It feels inescapable, but part of changing the tide is on you as much as us in the public eye.'

In 2022, Pugh hit back at 'vulgar' social media users who criticised her body after she posted photographs of herself wearing a sheer dress designed by Valentino's creative director Pierpaolo Piccioli to one of the brand's shows.

'What happened to you to be so content on being so loudly upset by the size of my boobs and body?' Pugh wrote at the time.
